core: A calorie is a unit of energy; the number on a food label is the energy in one serving, from all sources
Per-gram energy values: carbohydrate 4, protein 4, fat 9, alcohol 7 kcal/g; fat is the most energy-dense nutrient
A food-label Calorie is a kilocalorie (heat to raise 1 kg of water by 1 degree Celsius); labels use the short name
The body uses food energy in three broad ways: immediate use (function, digest, move), building (growth and repair), and storage of surplus
Energy-balance principle stated in one line: gain weight when calories in exceed calories out; the label's 2,000-calorie figure is a general guide, not a personal number
Label math: calories are per serving; servings per container matters; per-gram values can be checked against label totals
Honest framing: the calorie is a measuring tool, not a moral score
One original worked example reading a granola-bar label (arithmetic verified)
supporting: Alcoholic drinks carry calories that add up quickly and have little nutritional value (empty calories)
'Fat-free' and 'no added sugars' do not mean calorie-free
outOfScope: Energy-balance dynamics, weight-change mechanics, and calorie needs → nutrition:foundations:energy-balance (own topic; principle referenced only)
Metabolic pathways and metabolic rates → nutrition:foundations:metabolism (own topic)
Reading every part of the Nutrition Facts label → nutrition:foundations:nutrition-labels (own topic)
Portion-size guidance and measuring → nutrition:foundations:portion-sizes (own topic)

claims.claim: A calorie is a unit of energy, and the calories in food describe the amount of energy a food or drink provides to the body.

Carbohydrate and protein each supply about 4 calories per gram, fat about 9 calories per gram, and alcohol about 7 calories per gram; fat therefore carries more than double the energy of carbohydrate or protein per gram.
The calories used in nutrition measure the heat it takes to raise 1 kilogram of water by 1 degree Celsius, which is a kilocalorie; food labels state this same unit under the name 'Calories.'
Human bodies need calories to function, digest food, grow, and move, so food energy is used immediately, used for building and repair, and stored when it is not needed at the moment.

On the Nutrition Facts label, the Calorie number is the total energy from carbohydrate, fat, protein, and alcohol in one serving of the food; eating two servings means two times the calories shown (FDA example: 220 for one serving, 440 for two).

Body weight changes when the calories taken in from food and drinks differ from the calories the body uses through physical activity and daily living; balancing the two is the stated FDA guidance for a healthy body weight.
Alcoholic beverages contain calories that add up quickly, with a couple of drinks able to add 500 calories or more to a day's intake, and most alcoholic drinks have little to no nutritional value.

Worked example (author-constructed, arithmetic verified): a granola bar labeled 10 g fat, 22 g carbohydrate, and 3 g protein per serving totals 190 calories (90 + 88 + 12), matching its 190-Calorie label; two bars = 380; the six-bar box = 1,140; one and a half bars = 285.

sourceRecords.title: Calories on the Nutrition Facts Label
sourceRecords.notes: Verified 2026-08-22. States that Calories on the label is the total energy from all sources (carbohydrate, fat, protein, and alcohol) in a serving; serving sizes reflect what people typically eat and drink; calories shown in large bold type; guidance to balance calories eaten and drunk with calories the body uses; 2,000 calories a day as a general guide; FDA example of 220 calories for one serving and 440 for two; 'fat-free' and 'no added sugars' do not mean calorie-free. Content current as of 03/05/2024.

sourceRecords.title: OpenStax Nutrition (Nutrition for Nurses) 2e, Section 1.1: What Is Nutrition?
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture of 2024-04-12 (openstax.org blocks direct fetching). Provides the working calorie definition used in the lesson: 'Calories, which measure the amount of heat it takes to raise 1 kg of water by 1 degrees C, are used to indicate the amount of energy needed or ingested daily,' plus 'Human bodies need calories to function, digest food, grow, and move,' Table 1.1 macronutrient energy yield (carbohydrate 4, fat 9, protein 4 kcal/g), and the 2020-2025 DGA estimated calorie ranges (women 1,600-2,400; men 2,000-3,000). Book license forbids LLM ingestion; facts synthesized, prose original.

sourceRecords.title: OpenStax Nutrition (Nutrition for Nurses) 2e, Section 2.2: Fats
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture of 2024-04-12. Table 2.4 'Energy Contribution of Macronutrients' gives carbohydrate 4, fat 9, protein 4, water 0, and alcohol 7 calories per gram. Text confirms fat 'supplying more than double the caloric energy of carbohydrates or protein,' that alcohol provides calories but no vitamins, minerals, or fiber ('empty' calories), and that all fats provide about 9 calories per gram whether saturated or not. Book license forbids LLM ingestion; facts synthesized, prose original.

sourceRecords.title: Weight Control (Health Topic)
sourceRecords.notes: Verified 2026-08-22. Supplies the one-line energy-balance principle: 'You gain weight when you take in more calories (through food and drinks) than you use up from physical activity and daily living.' Weight-management mechanics and factors are explicitly out of scope and owned by the energy-balance topic.

sourceRecords.title: Calorie Count: Alcoholic Beverages (Patient Instruction)
sourceRecords.notes: Verified 2026-08-22. States that alcoholic beverages contain calories that add up quickly ('Going out for a couple of drinks can add 500 calories, or more, to your daily intake') and that most alcoholic drinks have little to no nutritional value. Supports the alcohol row of the per-gram table and the empty-calories idea.

sourceRecords.title: Protein in Diet (Medical Encyclopedia)
sourceRecords.notes: Verified 2026-08-22. States 'One gram of protein supplies 4 calories' and that protein should supply 10-35% of total calories for healthy adults. Independently corroborates the protein value in OpenStax Table 2.4.
